Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Mabel, an eighty‑year‑old African‑American pastor in a quiet Southern town, had lived a life of quiet devotion until the night she fled a war‑torn country in her early twenties. She was a young woman, hair still dark, carrying a small bundle of church supplies when the sky split with artillery fire. A nearby school was turned into a makeshift morgue, and the air was thick with the scent of gunpowder and blood. When her village was overrun, she slipped into a convoy of refugees, clutching a battered Bible. The convoy was ambushed by soldiers with rifles that glinted like knives in the twilight; a gunshot rang, and a shell tore through a canvas tarp, scattering her belongings into the mud. In that instant, Mabel felt as if she had been ripped from the present, the world flattening into a dream she could not shake. The memory of that night has remained with her, unbidden, whispering its dark refrain whenever the air shifts. The next time she stepped onto a city bus in her new town, the simple act of riding in public transport became a trigger that set off a cascade of distress. The low hum of the bus engine and the sight of a fellow passenger’s gun‑shaped backpack—an object that mirrored the weapons she had seen—reminded Mabel of the chaos on that night. In that moment she felt detached, as though the bus were a stage and she merely an actor watching from the sidelines. She avoided speaking to anyone, her voice hushed even in the quiet of her own mind, because the thought of reliving that terror in conversation seemed too painful. She wrapped herself in a long cloak, concealing her features as if a mask could ward off an unseen threat. Her avoidance of medical care—her reluctance to visit the clinic where a nurse once offered a comforting smile—further deepened her sense of isolation. The sudden jostling of a passenger’s chair, a quick shift in the bus’s trajectory, heightened her perception of an immediate threat, compelling her to watch everyone around her for any hint of hostility, and to glance over her shoulder repeatedly to ensure no one was following. Each of these responses was rooted in the terror that the bus ride rekindled; the triggers, therefore, seemed to lead directly into her maladaptive strategies, her perception of threat, and her negative appraisals of injustice and dehumanization. Because Mabel constantly perceived injustice—her past humiliation by foreign soldiers, the unacknowledged suffering of her family, and the indifferent gaze of strangers—she found herself withdrawing further. The belief that the world was unfair made her think that discussing the events would only bring more pain, reinforcing her avoidance of conversation. In turn, this avoidance fed a deeper conviction that anyone who saw her would perceive her as an object of pity or suspicion, thereby amplifying the sense that she was being watched, that danger lurked in every movement. The injustice she felt also sharpened the memory’s grip; she would recall the shell burst and the hiss of gunfire with such clarity that it felt almost unreal, as though the scene were a nightmare. The recurring memory, in turn, reminded her of the injustice, creating a loop that reinforced her triggers—any glimpse of a weapon, any sudden movement—would again set her on high alert. The negative appraisals also spurred her to keep her clothing concealed, a tangible way to protect herself from the indignity she feared she might suffer in the community. When Mabel’s mind inevitably drifted back to that night, the intrusive memory would spill over into her day, forcing her to check the rearview mirror with the urgency of a guard on patrol. She would hear echoes of the distant gunfire in her own head, an auditory reminder that the past was not over. These auditory recollections intensified her sense of threat, as if the echo were a warning of imminent danger. The heightened threat, in turn, made her more convinced of the world’s injustice and of her own vulnerability, deepening her negative appraisals. Her avoidance strategies—steering clear of conversations, donning long, opaque garments, shying away from the clinic—reinforced the memory’s persistence by preventing any opportunity for reframing or integration. Each avoidance act also brought her closer to feeling watched; she began to look behind her as soon as she stepped onto the street, her mind constantly scanning for potential threats. Thus the maladaptive strategies fed back into the cycle of memory, threat, and negative appraisal, tightening the loop that had become Mabel’s daily reality. Now, at eighty, Mabel sits in the quiet of her office, a pastoral chair that once held a congregation’s hopeful voices, and she looks up from a Bible she has held for decades. The decision to seek help came after a week of relentless bus rides that left her shaking, after a sudden check‑behind while crossing a dimly lit alley that triggered a feeling of being hunted, and after an intrusive recollection of gunfire that made her feel she had slipped back into that warzone. She fears that the memories will never cease, that the threat will always loom in the periphery of her life. Yet she also hopes that, with professional support, she might untangle the threads of her past from the present, learn to trust the safety of her own community, and perhaps once again speak freely of her story, without feeling the world’s injustice crushing her spirit.
